CausalChain: Radiotherapy → Tumor cell death releases neoantigens → Activation and expansion of precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells in STIE → Cancer stem cells and stroma secrete high levels of TGF‑β and IDO → TGF‑β/IDO recruit immunosuppressive cells (Tregs, MDSCs) and induce T cell exhaustion → Inhibition of PD‑1 alone is insufficient due to persistent suppression → Dual blockade of TGF‑β/IDO removes suppression → Leaves a reinvigorated precursor exhausted T cell pool that can be converted to active effectors via PD‑1 blockade.
Hypothesis: Dual inhibition of TGF‑β and IDO signaling when combined with radiotherapy and PD‑1 blockade will disrupt the CSC‐driven immunosuppressive niche in both the systemic and local tumor immune environments, thereby enabling the reactivation of precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells and enhancing the overall efficacy of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in tumors that are prone to hyperprogression.
Abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that therapeutic resistance and hyperprogressive disease during PD‐1 inhibitor immunotherapy may be a consequence of an immunosuppressive network that is driven by factors secreted by cancer stem cells (CSCs) and the tumor stroma. Radiotherapy can enhance immune response by releasing tumor neoantigens; however, the concomitant release of immunosuppressive mediators such as transforming growth factor‑β (TGF‑β) and indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase (IDO) can blunt the reinvigoration of precursor exhausted T cells from the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE), limiting the efficacy of checkpoint blockade. Here, we propose that a multi‐modal combinatorial approach, in which radiotherapy is coupled with dual inhibition of TGF‑β/IDO signaling and PD‑1 blockade, may reshape both the systemic and local tumor immune microenvironments (TIME). This strategy is expected to reduce regulatory T cell and myeloid‑derived suppressor cell recruitment, reprogram the immunosuppressive niche, and permit the conversion of precursor exhausted (Texp) CD8+ T cells into effective anti‑tumor effector cells.
